explanation: Fires on the verb (or its object/quantifier, e.g. 'all', 'av', 'e') right after a purpose or infinitive frame such as 'opportunity to', 'how to', 'exercises to', 'focus [all]', 'used to'. Strongest on the main verb after 'to' that names an action to be done ('present', 'test', 'refresh', 'improve', 'reduce'). Works across several languages. Weak on paragraph-ending periods and other words.

Fires in code and in technical strings on tokens right after an opening quote, bracket or import keyword, especially the start of a module or string literal in require('...'), import ... from "...", and Lisp quote marks; also on parts of identifiers and charset strings. Weak to nothing in ordinary prose.

Fires on structural tokens near the start of code files, docs and structured metadata: JSDoc @param tags, Rd \usage/\item, Go 'package' lines, file-header comment newlines, YAML 'bibliography: -' list dashes, subtitle timestamps and case captions ('Plaintiff-Appellee,v.'). In short, boilerplate or markup syntax at the head of a structured document. Weak in prose.

Fires on the LaTeX backslash that starts a command inside math mode ($\lambda, {\sqrt, _\Theta), and also on regex backslashes like \W. Strongest right after '{', '_', '^' or '$'. Weak activations land on subword pieces in the middle of long or foreign words.

Fires on word-internal subword pieces or closing tokens that finish a multi-token word or a fixed phrase, e.g. 'SOP[H]', 'sub[d]ural', 'Circuit [Judges]', 'no [way]', 'it [all]', '(RT[)]'. Strongest where the next token is largely predictable from the phrase or word so far. Mixed surface forms.

Fires on tokens inside descriptive expository noun phrases and lists, often a comma or 'and' joining list items ('skin and hair[,]', 'evens skin tone[, and]') or the head noun after a defining adjective ('the [main] cause', 'seaside [town]'). Typical of encyclopedic or product-description prose. The pattern is diffuse.

Fires on articles and determiners ('a', 'an', 'the') that follow a preposition inside idiomatic prepositional phrases ('at [a] distance', 'on [a] global scale', 'at [an] early age', 'on [a] daily basis', 'by [the] time'). Strongest when the article opens a fixed adverbial phrase. Weak on other tokens.

Fires on the token that completes a word or a highly predictable phrase in many unrelated contexts: 'PER CURI[AM]', 'Not [surprisingly]', 'document[.cookie]', 'bio[terror]ism', 'Saturdays and [Sundays]'. No shared semantic theme.

Fires on a particle or preposition that continues a multi-word construction after a subject or clause, especially ', [along] with', 'arising/coming [out] of', 'toward the [end] of', 'been [looking] for', 'What [say] you'. Strongest on 'along' in ', along with X'.

Fires on characters or subword pieces inside technical identifiers and codes: digits inside U.S. patent numbers ('5,3[8]1'), shell or compiler flags ('-exec', '-I', 'if [ test'), HTTP header names, and chemical name fragments ('m[ethyl]'). Pieces of compact technical strings, not words.
Fires mainly on the word 'settle' and its forms ('settled', 'settlement', 'Settlers', 'settle for/in/on') in any sense. Secondary hits are 'turn [around]', 'fewer [still]' and 'still' in general.

Fires on Romance-language (French, Spanish, Portuguese) proper names, accented words and nationality adjectives: 'Québec', 'Conservatoire', 'González', 'López', 'Café', 'Mexican', 'French', 'Colombian'. The token itself carries the signal, whether it appears in English or in foreign text.

Fires on tokens inside lists or numbered sequences and inside fragmented compound strings: list-section boundaries, roster entries, number pieces in years or IPs ('192.[1]68', '(1990–[2]009)'), and chemical-name pieces. No clear common function.

Fires on tokens in scientific or technical prose, mostly a preposition or the content word that completes a noun phrase ('in physiological and [pathological]', 'metall[urgical]', 'to the [south]', '\int[_{]'). Mixed contexts with no single predictable trigger.

Fires on the dash, final year digit or keyword in biographical lead lines: the '–' between birth and death dates, the last digit of a year in '(1900 - 199[0])', 'Notable [people] with the surname', '[births]', 'was [born]'. Specific to the opening of a Wikipedia-style person or surname article.

Fires on evaluative adjectives or adverbs of quality or difficulty, especially after 'how', 'as', 'a' or 'super' ('how [difficult]', 'as [smooth] as', 'easy and [secure]', 'a [tough] place', 'how [painful]'). Also fires on related nouns such as 'difficulty' and 'sharpness'.

Fires most strongly on 'pone' in PLOS ONE citation keys ('[@pone.0...'). Weaker hits are paragraph or section starts after a newline and number pieces inside reference IDs. Main job is citation-key tokens.

Fires on line-start tokens in config, metadata and manifest files (quotes and newlines in TOML, JSON, YAML, pom.xml), plus a separate hit on the subword 'prop'/'Pro' ('propria', 'propuesta', 'Prophecy').

Fires on words about recent change or time ('in [recent] years', '[new]', '[increasingly]', 'detox[ified]', 'modern[ization]', 'has [changed]', 'took [office]'). The theme is change over time or newness, but many hits are loose.

Fires on words about a machine or system running or operating ('operating [under] a load', 'turn [on]', 'would [run]', '[operating] frequency', 'during photograph[ing]', and the R Shiny 'output'/'render'). Mostly technical or patent prose about how a device works.

Fires on tokens in stock license-boilerplate phrases ('you may not [use] this file', 'with or [without] modification', 'except [in] compliance', 'NOT LIMITED [TO]') and other formulaic phrases ('Thanks in [advance]', '[if] you wish'). Strongest in Apache and BSD license headers.
